design: Written for the open pack from real history and geography; nothing comes from the original game. Sources: the ports' foundation, abandonment and change of hands as in the general histories of the Spanish Caribbean and of the buccaneers (Haring, "The Buccaneers in the West Indies in the XVII Century", 1910; Andrews, "The Spanish Caribbean: Trade and Plunder 1530-1630", 1978; Exquemelin, "De Americaensche Zee-Roovers", 1678), and the places' modern coordinates (degrees, the town's old centre or harbour), given in LINEAGE below. Which towns. An era shows the settlements that stood at some time in its first decade, [year, year + 10), with the nation that held them at the era's year: a career starts then and plays mostly that decade. So Curacao is Dutch from 1640 (taken 1634), Barbados English from 1620 (settled 1627), Jamaica English from 1660 (1655), Tortuga French from 1620 (the boucaniers, about 1630; Le Vasseur's fort, 1640). A town moved to a new site keeps its record (Nombre de Dios to Portobelo in 1597, Puerto Caballos to Santo Tomas in 1604, La Yaguana abandoned in 1605 and resettled by the French as Leogane, Jamaica's capital to Port Royal), so the same town keeps its "id" across eras. Stretches, for play. Every nation gets at least three home ports in every era, so each career has a governor to report to; where history has fewer, the era takes the real attempts and footholds of the time and, failing those, a colony a little earlier than it was. Each is marked "STRETCH" in LINEAGE. 1560: Fort Caroline (1564-65) beside San Agustin (1565), Charlesfort (1562-63); for England Drake's hidden Port Pheasant (1572), the Isla de Pinos where the English rovers watered (the 1570s-90s) and Bermuda (1612); for France Tortuga (settled about 1630) and for Holland Punta de Araya (the salt fleets, 1599), Curacao (1634) and St Eustatius (1636). 1600: Bermuda (the Sea Venture's castaways, 1609-10), the real English attempts on St Lucia (1605) and Grenada (1609), the Isla de Pinos again; Tortuga, Martinique and Guadeloupe French (1635); Punta de Araya (Dutch to 1605), Curacao and St Eustatius Dutch. 1620: Martinique and Guadeloupe French, St Maarten (1631) and Curacao Dutch. Where islands lie closer than three map cells, one town stands for them (no French Basseterre beside English St Christopher, no Saba beside St Eustatius). 48 at most an era; the least important (Tolu, San German, Baracoa, Coro, Tampico, Santo Tomas, Eleuthera, Montserrat in 1680) leave the crowded later eras. The fields, as the engine reads them (src/sim/sim.c, town.c, land.c, battle.c, prison.c, src/ui/screens.c): - x, y: the town's map cell (640 x 480 cells, 16 world pixels each). flags: 0x08 food, 0x04 goods, 0x02 sugar are a local product (half price at the merchant), 0x10 sugar wanted (twice its price), 0x40 TOWN_INLAND (reached on foot; its arrival picture is the land one); 0x20 and 0x80 are the player's information, clear at the start. - nation: who holds it at the era's year. - forts: 0-5, 12 guns each in the fort battle; 0 lets any ship in. soldiers: tens of men (the city information shows x 10); the monthly growth moves them a step toward (income + citizens) / 2. citizens: hundreds of inhabitants (x 100 in the city information); under 6 there is no governor; they size the merchant's purse and stock and the recruits. gold: the town's treasure, about a thousand pieces of eight each when sacked by surprise; wealth: 0-255, 64 a level (poor, modest, prosperous, wealthy), the merchant's prices and the shipwright's purse. The Spanish treasure ports are rich and strong, the young colonies and the buccaneer havens small and poor; the table below gives every value. - standing, garrison, family, barmaid: 0 (the player's history with the town, and the mark of a villain hiding there); governor: a repeatable draw 0-15, as a new governor's (bit 0 a niece rather than a daughter; the bits 0x20-0x80 are the player's doings). - id: the town's battle screens (screens/sea layer id, the land battle's screens/land layer id, both indexed by it), the same in every era: 0-60 for the towns that last, 61 and up (screens to 107) for the early footholds only. Inland towns use the ids the engine nudges toward the right coast when the player leaves their prison (src/sim/prison.c): Panama 43 (20 cells north, to the Caribbean side of the isthmus), Granada 45 (50 cells east, past Lake Nicaragua); the other inland towns avoid those ids. - land [x, y], party [x, y]: the land battle (15 x 15 cells of 32 pixels): the town, and where the attackers come ashore, on the side of the town's sea. fort [x, y], ship [x, y, heading]: the fort battle on the same 15 x 15 grid: the fort by the shore, the attacker coming in from the open water, heading for it (0-255, 0 north, clockwise). These follow one convention from the direction of the town's water (see battle_cells()), for the open battle screens to be drawn to. - sea [x, y, heading]: the map cell where a ship leaving the town starts, on open sea (no shallows, which wreck large ships), outside the town's arrival cells, heading 0-7 (x 32) to the open water: of the nearest such cells, the first with 16 cells of open sea straight ahead (else the longest such run), so a ship sailing straight out meets no shallows; 0, 0 for inland towns. Where a town's arrival cells lie across a strait (Maracaibo, between its lake and the Gulf), only the cells joined to the open sea without crossing any town's arrival cells are taken, so a ship leaving for the open sea does not sail straight back into the town it left. Every port must be reached from the open sea without crossing another town's arrival cells (a ship entering them stops at that town), or the build stops. - citymap [x, y]: the town's dot on the Map of the Caribbean, which shows the whole world at 0.75 from the screen's top-left: the cell times 0.75, rounded. - arrival: the cells where a ship or a party reaches the town: the 3 x 3 cells around each of its map tiles, and for a coastal town, when those hold no open sea joined to the main water, the cells on toward it (at most 16). No cell belongs to two towns. No shallows (the map's reefs) lie within HARBOUR (8) cells of a town's tiles or arrival cells, so its approaches are safe for every ship; the build stops otherwise. Placement. Each town's real coordinates go through _geo.lonlat_to_world() and snap to the nearest fitting cell of the bare map (world_map.base_grid()'s tile terrain): a coastal town on a cell with some land (an eighth, preferably half) within four cells of a cell with open sea of the main water (one 4-connected body of sea pixels holding the open Caribbean, so a ship can sail in without crossing shallows), the nearer the better; where shallows lie between, its arrival cells run out across them to that open sea. An islet the map's tiles drew as shallows (Providence) keeps its town there, the house tile giving it land. An inland town sits on land with no such sea within a cell. The towns are placed most important first, each at least three cells (Chebyshev) from every town it shares an era with, so arrival cells never touch. Map tiles. The open tile sheet's tiles with a house (world_map's BUILDINGS): 68-79 a house on a shore, the twelve of them the coast on different sides, and 123-127 and 255 a house inland. Each town cell takes the building tile whose terrain best matches the geography there and its four neighbours' edges (the costs of world_map's seams), so the shore runs on. A town of 4000 people or more in the era (citizens 40) gets a second house on the neighbouring land cell that fits one best, so the big ports read as cities. Routes. The treasure fleet follows the Spanish fleets' circuit, as one convoy: in at Puerto Rico and Santo Domingo, the galeones at Cartagena, the Isthmus fair (Nombre de Dios, Portobelo from 1597) and Cartagena again, the flota at Veracruz and Campeche, all meeting at Havana and leaving by the Florida channel past San Agustin. The silver train follows the treasure by land: Peru's silver over the Camino Real from Panama (by Chagres) to the Isthmus port, then the Main's treasure roads east, Cartagena (New Granada's gold), Santa Marta, Rio de la Hacha (pearls), Maracaibo and Gibraltar (cacao), Coro, Caracas and Cumana. A stop missing from an era is left out; the engine passes over the towns not Spanish. This era: 44 towns (spain 34, england 4, france 3, holland 3).
